challenges.brief: A serif blog post with a pull quote, a six-bar chart and a ten-row table.

items.label: Heading
items.value: What we learned from a year of four-day weeks; 40px, bold, line-height 1.2, 12px gap below

items.label: Byline
items.value: By Maya Ortiz · March 4, 2026 · 7 min read (non-breaking space in 7 min); Verdana 15px, #78716c, 32px gap below

items.label: Paragraphs
items.value: 18px, line-height 1.5, #44403c, 20px gap below; curly quotes and apostrophes throughout

items.label: Paragraph 1
items.value: Last March we tried something our board called “brave” and our accountant called “unwise”: every team would work Monday to Thursday, with Friday off and no cut in pay. We promised to measure everything and to stop if it didn’t work.

items.label: Paragraph 2
items.value: We expected output to fall. Instead, most teams shipped slightly more, and the number of late projects dropped by a third. The biggest change was not speed but focus: people stopped filling Fridays with meetings that could have been an email.

items.label: Quote
items.value: “I get more done in four focused days than I used to in five scattered ones.”

items.label: Style
items.value: Margin 28px 0, 20px left padding, 4px #b45309 left border, 22px italic #78350f

items.label: Paragraph 3
items.value: That line came from our support lead, and it summed up the survey. Nobody wanted to go back. (this sentence bold) Even the two teams whose numbers dipped asked to keep the schedule and fix the problems instead.

items.label: Heading
items.value: The numbers; 26px, bold, margin 36px 0 16px

items.value: Ten years ago, the sleeper train looked finished. Budget airlines had taken the routes, the carriages were old, and operators were cutting services every winter. Today new lines open every season, and many of them sell out weeks in advance.

items.label: Paragraph 2
items.value: What changed was not the trains themselves but the travellers. Families, remote workers and people avoiding short flights now treat a night on the rails as part of the trip rather than a cost of it.
